5 min read
Just now

--

A product manager once put a slide in front of us with a single sentence on it, in a font too large for how little it actually explained: a 100 millisecond delay costs Amazon 1% of revenue. Under it, a second line from a different deck entirely: every second Walmart shaves off improves conversion by 2%. And she asked the obvious next question, so why hasn’t the team fixed our load time yet, and none of us in that room could actually answer her, because none of us could say, out loud, what our load time even was.
We had a dashboard. The dashboard said 1.8 seconds. But 1.8 seconds of what, we didn’t know, and neither, it turned out, did the dashboard.
These two numbers get quoted in every performance deck, every stakeholder pitch, every why we need to fix the site email, and we repeat them without ever asking the obvious question first. A hundred milliseconds of what, exactly. What is the browser doing during that stretch, and which part of it did Amazon and Walmart actually measure?
Page load sounds like a single event, and it is not, it is a name we slap onto a sequence of five distinct moments in the browser’s timeline, and none of them happen at the same time, and almost nobody quoting the number knows which one they mean.
The clock starts before anyone sees anything
